title: Why Do Aircraft Carriers Catch Jets With Cables?
description:
A fighter jet lands at around two hundred and forty kilometres per hour. On a normal airport, it needs a runway more than a kilometre long to stop. On an aircraft carrier, it has about one hundred metres. So the ship catches it, with a steel cable, and stops it in around two seconds. Today, ten parts of an aircraft carrier, and why each one exists.

Machine Reverse takes apart the machines you see every day and explains, part by part, why each one exists. This video covers 10 parts.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
1:03 1. The arresting wires
2:10 2. The tailhook
3:17 3. The full throttle landing
4:18 4. The catapult
5:32 5. The blast deflector
6:29 6. The angled deck
7:35 7. The landing lights
8:48 8. The island
9:55 9. The folding wings
11:00 10. The coloured shirts
12:07 The verdict

Sources:
- Arresting gear, wires, third-wire target, bolters: Wikipedia, "Arresting gear" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arresting_gear
- Tailhooks: Wikipedia, "Tailhook" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tailhook
- Catapults, steam catapult (Colin Mitchell), EMALS on USS Gerald R. Ford: Wikipedia, "Aircraft catapult" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aircraft_catapult and "Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electromagnetic_Aircraft_Launch_System
- Jet blast deflector: Wikipedia, "Jet blast deflector" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jet_blast_deflector
- Angled flight deck (Royal Navy, 1950s): Wikipedia, "Angled flight deck" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angled_flight_deck
- Optical landing system and mirror landing aid: Wikipedia, "Optical landing system" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_landing_system
- Island and Queen Elizabeth class twin islands: Wikipedia, "Island (aircraft carrier)" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Island_(aircraft_carrier) and "Queen Elizabeth-class aircraft carrier" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth-class_aircraft_carrier
- Folding wings: Wikipedia, "Folding wing" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folding_wing
- Flight deck crew colours: Wikipedia, "Flight deck" https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flight_deck and US Navy https://www.navy.mil/
